summary: Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection modifies IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and Stateless Address Autoconfiguration. It aims to cut address configuration delays when no conflict exists, limit disruption when one does, and stay interoperable with unmodified hosts and routers. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of waiting to be sure nobody else has your address, you start using it right away and back off if someone complains.

questions: what is an optimistic address in ipv6
how does ipv6 duplicate address detection work
subtitle: Lets an IPv6 host start using a new address right away while it checks for duplicates in the background.

tldr.problem: Standard Duplicate Address Detection makes a host wait before it can use a new IPv6 address, which is too slow for nodes that often change their network attachment, even though a collision is very unlikely.
tldr.mechanism: The host marks the address Optimistic and uses it immediately, with restrictions that keep it from overwriting neighbors' Neighbor Cache entries, and it gives the address up if a duplicate is detected.
tldr.outcome: Address configuration is faster in the usual no-collision case and disruption is limited when there is a collision. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7527.

today: RFC 4429 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7527; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem with Waiting
sections.content:
Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) modifies IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 2461) and Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 2462). It rests on the observation that DAD is far more likely to succeed than fail, so waiting for it to finish is usually wasted time.

The RFC says a growing number of nodes need continuous network access while frequently changing their network attachment. An optimized method needs to interoperate with current nodes, remove the RetransTimer delay, not raise the probability of collision, improve resolution of collisions and minimize disruption. Simply shortening RetransTimer is not enough, because values long enough to guarantee detection are too long for time-critical services.

It is not the aim of the memo to improve the security or robustness of DAD, only to make it faster.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost nobody ever has the same name tag as you, so waiting around to check every time is a waste. This idea lets you start right away.

sections.title: The Optimistic Address State
sections.content:
RFC 2462 already has Tentative addresses (uniqueness being checked, not usable), Preferred addresses and Deprecated addresses (available, but not to be used if another suitable one exists). This memo adds an Optimistic address: assigned and available for use, subject to restrictions, while DAD is still running.

Components of the IPv6 stack should treat an Optimistic address like a Deprecated one, so it is only used as a source address when no other suitable address is available. Implementations that keep states as flags can set 'Deprecated' whenever 'Optimistic' is set. When DAD completes without a problem, the address becomes Preferred or Deprecated according to RFC 2462.

Optimistic DAD SHOULD only be used for addresses built from a most likely unique interface identifier, generated randomly, made by a well-distributed hash function, or assigned by DHCPv6. It SHOULD NOT be used for manually entered addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: An optimistic address is a name tag you may wear, but you should prefer a tag you are sure about whenever you have one.

sections.title: Rules That Avoid Disruption
sections.content:
The main danger is that the new node overwrites its neighbors' Neighbor Cache entries for an address that really belongs to someone else. The rules prevent that:

  • Neighbor Advertisements for an Optimistic address are sent with the Override flag cleared (O=0).
  • A node MUST NOT use an Optimistic address as the source of a Neighbor Solicitation, because the Source Link-Layer Address Option could disturb caches. DAD solicitations come from the unspecified address, without that option.
  • A Router Solicitation MUST NOT carry a source link-layer address option from an Optimistic address.
  • A node MUST NOT reply to a Neighbor Solicitation for an Optimistic address that comes from the unspecified address. Such a solicitation means the address is a duplicate, and it MUST be deconfigured as for a Tentative address.

On the autoconfiguration side, a host MAY configure a new address as Optimistic, SHOULD NOT delay before sending Neighbor Solicitations, and must flag the address as Optimistic. A host that does not know its router's link-layer address SHOULD NOT use an Optimistic address, and a router SHOULD NOT configure one.
sections.plainLanguage: While you are wearing a not-yet-confirmed name tag, you must not tell people to change the tag they have written down for someone else. You may only listen and answer politely.

sections.title: How It Plays Out
sections.content:
In the simple case the Optimistic address is unused. The Optimistic Node sends a Neighbor Solicitation from :: and nobody answers. It already knows the router's link-layer address from the Router Advertisement, so communication can begin at once, and after the DAD delay the address becomes Preferred or Deprecated.

In the collision case, the solicitation changes no neighbor's cache. Any Neighbor Advertisements the node sent had O=0, so they did not override entries, though a colliding entry may have gone to state STALE, which standard Neighbor Unreachability Detection can recover. When the rightful owner sends an advertisement defending the address, the node stops using it and deconfigures it. Meanwhile it may have sent packets that identify it as the owner, such as Mobile IPv6 Binding Updates, which can break connections and misdirect traffic to the real owner. That is why Optimistic DAD should be used only where collisions are very unlikely.

A node cannot send Neighbor Solicitations from an Optimistic address, so it forwards packets to a neighbor through its default router and relies on an ICMP Redirect to learn the neighbor's link-layer address. If the router does not include its link-layer address in Router Advertisements, the node MUST leave the address Tentative.
sections.plainLanguage: Usually nothing happens and you simply carry on. If it turns out someone else owns the tag, they shout, you take yours off, and a few messages might have gone to the wrong person.

sections.title: Working with Standard Nodes
sections.content:
Once an address has finished DAD it behaves like any normal address, so interoperability only matters while it is Optimistic. If an Optimistic Node tries to configure an address that a Standard Node is still checking, the Standard Node sees the solicitation and deconfigures it. If a node tries to take an address that an Optimistic Node holds, the Optimistic Node sees the solicitation and deconfigures it.

Optimistic DAD has the same weaknesses as standard DAD: duplicates are not guaranteed to be detected if packets are lost. Raising DupAddrDetectTransmits above 1 reduces that probability for both. The scheme also depends on the router including link-layer address options in advertisements and being willing to redirect traffic; where it does not, behavior reverts to that of Standard DAD.
sections.plainLanguage: It plays fine with everyone else. If two people claim the same tag, one of them notices and backs off.

sections.title: Security and Collision Odds
sections.content:
The memo does not fix existing security concerns with Neighbor Discovery and autoconfiguration, and does not significantly add to them. It adds no new threats if Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) is used. Transient problems remain: a router that solicits for the address may accept the Optimistic Node's answer and queue packets to it, and the node can inject packets that appear to come from the legitimate owner.

Appendix A estimates collision odds for randomly chosen interface identifiers drawn from 2^62 possibilities. For example, with 500 nodes the upper bound is 5.4e-14, and with 500000 nodes it is 5.4e-08. For one node that moves into a network of 50000 nodes once per minute for 100 years, the probability of causing or suffering a collision is a little over 1 in a million.
sections.plainLanguage: It does not make the old safety problems worse. And the chance of two people picking the same random tag is tiny, even in a very big crowd.
